figureObjective: Summarize how source-observer approach raises and separation lowers observed sound frequency in a material medium.

claims.text: Approach increases observed sound frequency and separation decreases it through wavefront spacing or encounter-rate changes.
The schematic uses separate nonrelativistic sound cases and does not report measured speed, loudness, or distance.

anchors.exactQuote: The Doppler effect is a change in the observed pitch of a sound, due to relative motion between the source and the observer.
In general, then, relative motion of source and observer toward one another increases the perceived frequency. Relative motion apart decreases the perceived frequency.

anchors.location: OpenStax Physics 14.3, equations 14.11 and 14.12; PDF pages 447-448
anchors.normalizedEquation: moving source: f_obs = f_s v_w/(v_w +/- v_s); moving observer: f_obs = f_s (v_w +/- v_obs)/v_w

elements.meaning: Sound source moving or stationary relative to the medium.
Wavefront spacing in the material medium.

allowedVariation.rule: Stationary, approach, and separation cases may be columns or rows if source and observer motion remain distinct.
Colors may distinguish cases but may not encode frequency or loudness without evidence.
Generic vehicle, loudspeaker, listener, and road icons may establish roles but do not encode measurements.

mutations.description: Present the bounded sound equations as universal for light or relativistic speeds.
Show tighter wavefront spacing while labeling the observed frequency lower.
Use ring opacity, thickness, or a speedometer badge as measured loudness, frequency, or speed.
